# Summary of Information on John L. Pollock
John L. Pollock (1940–2012) was a philosopher and cognitive scientist known primarily for his foundational work in defeasible reasoning and epistemology. His 1974 book *Knowledge and Justification* established him as a significant figure in epistemology by framing knowledge norms as defeasible—subject to exceptions and revision—thereby addressing issues like the Gettier problem through ceteris paribus conditions. Pollock's epistemological approach was innovative in integrating defeasible reasoning into mainstream philosophy.
Pollock made major contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of OSCAR, an AI system embodying his theories of defeasible reasoning and cognitive architecture, including intentions, problem-solving, and decision-making. OSCAR was a LISP-based program notable for its interest-driven reasoning and efficiency grounded in avoiding "uninteresting" conclusions. His 1987 paper “Defeasible reasoning” and his conceptions of "undercutting" and "rebutting" defeat have become standard in defeasible reasoning literature. Pollock held faculty positions at several universities, most notably at the University of Arizona, where he co-founded the Cognitive Science Program. His doctoral work at UC Berkeley, under Ernest Adams, laid the groundwork for his lifelong focus on defeasible reasoning.
